title: Printing and Formatting
intro: `println!`, `format!` and `write!` share one mini-language inside the `{}`: width, alignment, precision, hex. Two traits decide how a value prints. `Display` (`{}`) is for people, and you write it yourself. `Debug` (`{:?}`) is for developers, and `#[derive(Debug)]` writes it for you.

coming_from.go: `{}` uses `Display`, close to your `String()` method, and `{:?}` uses `Debug`, which is what `%+v` prints for a struct with no `String()`. Go has one hook (`%v`, `%+v` and `%s` all call `String()`); Rust has two traits, and `{:?}` never uses your `Display`. Go prints any struct by default, but Rust only prints types that implement one of these traits.
coming_from.kotlin: `Display` is your `toString()` override, and `#[derive(Debug)]` is like the `toString` a data class writes for you. A Rust struct has neither until you add one, and width and precision go inside `{}` (`{n:>6}`) instead of `"%6d".format(n)`.
coming_from.python: The mini-language is close to Python's: `{n:>6}`, `{n:06}`, `{n:#x}`, with differences the page lists. `Display` is `__str__` and `Debug` is `__repr__`, but Rust has no default for either, and `{:.2}` means two decimal places, like Python's `.2f`, not two significant digits.
coming_from.typescript: `format!` is a template literal, and `{n:>6}` does what `padStart(6)` does. `Display` is your `toString()`, and `{:?}` is like `console.log(obj)`, but only for types with `#[derive(Debug)]`.
coming_from.java: `impl Display` is your `toString()`, and `#[derive(Debug)]` is like the `toString` a `record` writes for you. The format string is checked at compile time, where `String.format` checks it at run time.
coming_from.csharp: `impl Display` is overriding `ToString()`. `#[derive(Debug)]` is close to the `ToString` a `record` gives you, but only for `{:?}`: `Display` has no default. `{n:>6}` is `{n,6}`. C# checks the arguments of `$"..."` at compile time but not the letter after the colon (`$"{n:Q}"` fails at run time); Rust checks both.
coming_from.c: `{:>6}`, `{:.2}` and `{:#x}` cover what `%6d`, `%.2f` and `%#x` do, but the argument type comes from the value, so a letter that disagrees with the argument is a compile error. `impl Display` is your `money_str` function, and `derive(Debug)` writes the field-by-field print for you.
coming_from.cpp: The `{}` mini-language is almost the same as C++20 `std::format`, and `impl Display` is a `std::formatter` specialization. The difference is `#[derive(Debug)]`: Rust writes a developer print for your struct, where C++ makes you write `operator<<` by hand.

notes: Inside `{}`: `>6` right-aligns in 6 columns, `<6` left, `^6` centers, `06` pads with zeros, `.2` is decimal places, `x`/`b`/`e` are hex, binary and scientific, and `#` adds the `0x`/`0b` prefix.
You can name variables right in the braces: `{n:>6}`, `{price}`. Expressions like `{a + b}` aren't allowed; pass them as arguments instead.

Implementing `Display` decides how your type prints with `{}`, much like `toString()` or `__str__` in other languages. You also get `.to_string()` for free once `Display` exists. A width such as `{:>8}` reaches your `fmt` as data, and it is ignored unless your code uses it (`f.pad`).

`write!(f, ...)` inside `fmt` writes into the `Formatter`, which wraps the real destination. `Display` takes a `Formatter` instead of returning a `String`, so the text can go into stdout, a `String` or a buffer you own.
`{:?}` works on anything that implements `Debug`, and nearly every std type does: Vec, HashMap, Option, Result, tuples. Add `#[derive(Debug)]` to your own types and you're done.
`eprintln!` works like `println!` but prints to stderr. `print!` and `eprint!` don't add a newline.

The format string is checked at compile time. A wrong letter, a missing argument or a typo like `{nmae}` is a compile error. Go builds the mistake and writes it into the output, and C's `printf` has undefined behaviour; C++20 `std::format` checks at compile time too.

gotcha.title: Printing your own struct with {}
gotcha.looks_fine: `fmt.Println(p)` prints `{1 2}`. Every value in Go has a default print form, and so does a Kotlin data class.
gotcha.rust_sees: `{}` uses the `Display` trait, and Rust never writes `Display` for you. It can't guess whether a point should look like `(1, 2)`, `1,2` or `x=1 y=2`.
gotcha.why: Display is the version your users see, so Rust makes you write it. For a quick look while debugging, `#[derive(Debug)]` plus `{:?}` gives you `Point { x: 1, y: 2 }` with one line of code. For real output, implement `Display`, as in the fix.

go.says: Go runs this and prints {1 2}. Every struct has a default format, so you never have to write one.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints Point(x=1, y=2), because a data class writes `toString` for you. A plain class would print something like `Point@1b6d3586`.

python.says: Python prints Point(x=1, y=2), because `@dataclass` writes a `__repr__` for you. A plain class without one prints something like `<__main__.Point object at 0x7f...>`.
python.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int


p = Point(1, 2)
print(p)

typescript.says: Prints Point { x: 1, y: 2 }. `console.log` shows any object's fields. Putting it in a template literal instead, `${p}`, would print [object Object].

java.says: A record writes `toString` for you, so this prints Point[x=1, y=2]. A plain class would print something like Point@1b6d3586 unless you override `toString`.

csharp.says: A record writes `ToString` for you, so this prints Point { X = 1, Y = 2 }. A plain class would only print its type name, Point, unless you override `ToString`.

c.says: gcc with `-Wall` (the runner's flag) warns that `%d` wants an int, not a `struct Point`, but builds it anyway; with no flags it says nothing. It printed `1` here, just the bits of `x`; passing the wrong type to printf is undefined behaviour.

python.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pprint import pprint


class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents: int):
        self.cents = cents

    # __str__: how Money looks with print and f"{}"
    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return f"${self.cents // 100}.{self.cents % 100:02}"


@dataclass  # writes __repr__ for you, like derive(Debug)
class Item:
    name: str
    qty: int


n = 42
print(f"[{n:>6}] [{n:<6}] [{n:^6}] [{n:06}]")
print(f"{3.14159:.2f} {1234.5:e} {n:#x} {n:#b}")

price = Money(1999)
print(f"total: {price}")

label = f"{price} each"  # an f-string builds a str
print(f"{label} ({len(label)} chars)")

item = Item("pen", 3)
print(f"{item.qty} x {item.name}")
print(f"{item!r}")       # repr, written by @dataclass
